question: In Mongolia, how many years longer was female than male life expectancy at birth in 2019?

[Vision description] This is a grouped bar chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, by WHO regions and globally, for the years 2000 and 2020.

The chart has three panels, stacked vertically, representing "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female".
The y-axis for all panels is "Prevalence (%)", ranging from 0 to 70 in increments of 10.
The x-axis for each panel shows different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
Within each region/global category, there are two bars: a blue bar representing the year 2000 and an orange bar representing the year 2020.

Data values are as follows:

**Both sexes:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 17.9%, 2020: 10.3%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 28.0%, 2020: 16.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 27.2%, 2020: 18.6%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 34.6%, 2020: 25.3%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 50.4%, 2020: 29.0%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 27.9%, 2020: 24.6%
*   **Global:** 2000: 32.7%, 2020: 22.3%

**Male:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 28.7%, 2020: 17.8%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 35.5%, 2020: 21.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 44.1%, 2020: 33.0%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 46.5%, 2020: 32.9%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 68.2%, 2020: 46.6%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 50.8%, 2020: 46.4%
*   **Global:** 2000: 49.3%, 2020: 36.7%

**Female:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 7.1%, 2020: 2.8%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 20.6%, 2020: 11.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 10.2%, 2020: 4.2%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 22.6%, 2020: 17.4%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 32.5%, 2020: 11.3%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 5.0%, 2020: 2.8%
*   **Global:** 2000: 16.2%, 2020: 7.8%

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Both sexes" was in the South-East Asia Region (50.4%), and the lowest was in the African Region (17.9%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Male" was in the South-East Asia Region (68.2%), and the lowest was in the African Region (28.7%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).
*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. Globally, the current tobacco use prevalence

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

**Axes and Legend:**
* **Y-axis:** Anaemia prevalence (%) ranging from 0 to 50 in increments of 5.
* **X-axis:** Years from 2000 to 2019.
* **Legend categories (severity levels):**
  * Severe anaemia (Red)

  * Mild anaemia (Blue)

**Printed Data Values:**

* **Severe anaemia (red series):**
  * 2000: 1.7%
  * 2015: 1.1%
  * 2019: 1.0%

* **Moderate anaemia (yellow series):**
  * 2000: 14.1%
  * 2015: 12.2%
  * 2019: 12.7%

* **Mild anaemia (blue series):**
  * 2000: 15.5%
  * 2015: 15.5%
  * 2019: 16.2%

*(Note: Data values for years 2001 through 2014 and 2016 through 2018 are not explicitly labelled on the chart.)*

**Main Comparisons and Trends:**
* **Mild anaemia** accounts for the largest proportion of total prevalence throughout the period, followed by **moderate anaemia**, while **severe anaemia** makes up the smallest proportion.
* **Severe anaemia** shows a slight downward trend over time, declining from 1.7% in 2000 to 1.1% in 2015 and 1.0% in 2019.
* **Moderate anaemia** decreases from 14.1% in 2000 to a low of 12.2% in 2015 before rising slightly to 12.7% in 2019.
* **Mild anaemia** remains steady at 15.5% between 2000 and 2015, then increases to 16.2% in 2019.
* Total overall anaemia prevalence (the top of the stacked area) slightly decreases from 2000 through around 2012–2014 before rising again toward 2019.

Although the global prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15–49 years decreased slightly from 2000 [31.2% (UI: 28.7–34.1)] to 2019 [29.9% (UI: 27.0–32.8)], the total number affected increased considerably due to population growth – from 492.9 million in 2000 to 570.8 million in 2019. Prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than non-pregnant women [29.6% UI: 26.6–32.5)]. Globally, the prevalence of mild anaemia increased slightly from 15.5% (UI: 14.2–17.3) in 2000 to 16.2% (UI: 14.9–17.6) in 2019, while moderate anaemia declined slightly from 14.1% (UI: 12.4–16.1) in 2000 to 12.7% (UI: 10.6–14.8) in 2019, as did severe anaemia

* **2004:** WHO co-established the UN Road Safety Collaboration to prevent road traffic injuries
* **2005:** The International Health Regulations are revised
* **2006:** WHO Child Growth Standards are launched to help every child grow in an equitable way

Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020
[Text layer in figure] Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020 Not applicable No data available <20 20–99 100–299 300–499 500–999 ۽эььь (per 100 000 live births) Maternal mortality ratio 0 2000 4000 1000 km Source: Ref. (1).
[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020".

The map displays the maternal mortality ratio (per 100 000 live births) for countries and areas worldwide in 2020.

The legend categories for the maternal mortality ratio are:
- ≥1000 (dark red)
- 500–999 (red)
- 300–499 (dark pink)
- 100–299 (medium pink)
- 20–99 (light pink)
- <20 (very light pink)
- No data available (light grey)
- Not applicable (grey)

A scale bar indicates distances in kilometers: 0, 1000, 2000, 4000 km.

The highest maternal mortality ratios (≥1000, dark red) are concentrated in Central Africa, including countries like Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia. Other countries in this category include Afghanistan and Yemen.

Countries with ratios between 500–999 (red) are also predominantly in Africa, such as Niger, Mali, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Sudan. Some countries in South Asia, like Pakistan, also fall into this category.

The lowest maternal mortality ratios (<20, very light pink) are observed across North America (Canada, United States), most of Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of East Asia (e.g., Japan, South Korea). Many countries in South America also show lower ratios, generally in the 20–99 or 100–299 range.

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland, Western Sahara, and some parts of Central Asia. "Not applicable" (grey) is shown for areas like the Arctic.

Overall, the map clearly shows a strong geographical disparity, with the highest maternal mortality ratios concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, while North America, Europe, and Oceania generally have the lowest ratios.

Figure 1.2 shows countries and areas for which estimates are available. In 2020, 13 countries had a maternal mortality ratio that was very high (between 500 and 999) or extremely high (over 1000). Of these countries, 11 are in the African Region and two are in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. In total, 117 countries and areas had a maternal mortality ratio below 100 deaths per 100 000 live births, 60 of which had a very low maternal mortality ratio (below 20).
Disparities may also occur within countries, with maternal mortality ratio levels varying across subnational regions and places of residence, or by socioeconomic status such as income and educational levels, and by other social determinants such as race and ethnicity.
Key issues and trends in global health

[Vision description] Figure 1.1 Maternal mortality ratio and the average annual rate of reduction by WHO region, 2000–2020

This is a bar and scatter plot showing the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) and maternal mortality ratio (MMR) for different WHO regions.

The x-axis lists the WHO regions: European Region, Western Pacific Region, Region of the Americas, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and African Region.

The left y-axis represents the Average annual rate of reduction (ARR), %, ranging from -4.0% to 8.0%.
The right y-axis represents the MMR (maternal deaths per 100 000 live births), ranging from 0 to 800.

The legend categories are:

- ARR 2016–2020 (orange bars)

- MMR, 2020 (purple dots)

Data values:

  - ARR 2016–2020: -2.4%

  - ARR 2016–2020: -2.8%
  - MMR, 2000: 60

Region of the Americas:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 1.0%
  - ARR 2016–2020: -3.6%
  - MMR, 2000: 70
  - MMR, 2020: 60
South-East Asia Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 6.1%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 4.5%
  - MMR, 2000: 380
  - MMR, 2020: 130
Eastern Mediterranean Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 3.8%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 1.9%
  - MMR, 2000: 390
  - MMR, 2020: 190
African Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 1.9%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 1.8%
  - MMR, 2000: 790
  - MMR, 2020: 540

Main comparisons and trends:
- The South-East Asia Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 (6.1%) and also the highest positive ARR from 2016–2020 (4.5%).
- The European Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 among regions with negative ARR in 2016-2020.
- The Region of the Americas had the most negative ARR from 2016–2020 (-3.6%).
- The African Region had the highest MMR in both 2000 (790) and 2020 (540).
- The European Region had the lowest MMR in both 2000 (20) and 2020 (10).
- All regions showed a decrease in MMR from 2000 to 2020.
- European Region, Western Pacific Region, and Region of the Americas experienced a negative ARR from 2016–2020, indicating an increase in maternal mortality during this period.

The maternal mortality ratio levels, as well as the rates of progress and slowdown, have been uneven across WHO regions (Figure 1.1). The WHO South-East Asia Region maintained the fastest reduction rate during the MDG era and the first five years of the SDG era, reducing the maternal mortality ratio from 372 (UI: 336–423) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2000 to 117 (UI: 106–133) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2020. The African Region, while keeping the ARR relatively stable at 2.0% for the past two decades, continued to have the highest maternal mortality ratio. The Region of the Americas, the Western Pacific Region and the European Region saw a trend reversal, with the maternal mortality ratio levels increasing
between 2016 and 2020 after having decreased during the MDG era. However, the levels of the maternal mortality ratio have remained low (below 100 deaths per 100 000 maternal deaths) since 2000.

3. World Population Prospects 2022. New York (NY): United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs; 2022 (https:// population.un.org/wpp/, accessed 1 April 2023).

[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.6 Under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, by country/area, 2021". The map displays two types of mortality rates for countries and areas worldwide in 2021.

The "Under-five mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by color-coded regions:
- >75: Dark purple
- 51-75: Purple
- 26-50: Pink
- ≤25: Light orange
- No data available: Light grey
- Not applicable: Dark grey

The "Neonatal mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by circles of varying sizes and colors:
- 40: Largest red circle
- 29: Medium red circle
- 18: Small red circle
- 12: Medium green circle
- 1: Smallest green circle

The map shows that countries in sub-Saharan Africa generally have the highest under-five mortality rates (>75 and 51-75, dark purple and purple regions) and also the highest neonatal mortality rates (largest red circles, 40 and 29). Examples include Chad, Central African Republic, Somalia, and Nigeria.

Conversely, most countries in North America, Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia have the lowest under-five mortality rates (≤25, light orange regions) and the lowest neonatal mortality rates (smallest green circles, 1 and 12). Examples include Canada, United States, most of Western Europe, Australia, and Japan.

Some countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, such as India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, show a mix of pink (26-50) and light orange (≤25) for under-five mortality, with varying neonatal mortality rates, including some red circles (18 and 29).

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland and parts of the Sahara desert. "Not applicable" (dark grey) is shown for some small island nations and territories.

Child mortality
2 Child mortality statistics are presented here with 90% uncertainty intervals.
Child survival is an important marker of human development – it has been one of the main drivers of increasing global life expectancy over the past 75 years. The international community committed to reducing mortality among the youngest children, setting the SDG target to reduce neonatal mortality (i.e. mortality among newborn babies during the first month of life) by 2030 to at least as low as 12 per 1000 live births, and setting the under-five mortality target (i.e. mortality among children under 5 years of age) for the same period to at least as low as 25 per 1000 live births.
Levels and trends in mortality among children under five years of age

Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. The South-East Asia Region saw a big decline in deaths as the number of neonatal and post-neonatal under-five deaths dropped by 65% and 78%, respectively, between 2000 and 2021.

(4).
[Vision description] This is a stacked area chart titled "Figure 1.5 Trends in neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths, by WHO region, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Deaths (millions)" ranging from 0 to 10. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.

The chart is divided into two main stacked sections:
1.  "Neonatal deaths (0–28 days)" at the bottom.
2.  "Post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months)" on top of the neonatal deaths.

Each of these two sections is further subdivided by WHO region, represented by different colors in the legend:
*   African Region (red)
*   South-East Asia Region (purple)
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green)
*   Region of the Americas (light blue)
*   European Region (orange)
*   Western Pacific Region (yellow)

There are also two global trend lines:
*   Global under-five deaths (solid purple line)
*   Global neonatal deaths (dashed purple line)

The chart shows a clear downward trend in both neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths from 2000 to 2021.

In 2000, the total global under-five deaths were approximately 10 million. By 2021, this figure had decreased to approximately 5 million.

For neonatal deaths (0–28 days):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 3.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.2 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region contribute the largest proportions to neonatal deaths throughout the period.

For post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 6.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.8 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region also contribute the largest proportions to post-neonatal under-five deaths.

The overall trend for both categories and all regions is a decrease in deaths over the 21-year period. The African Region consistently shows the largest number of deaths in both categories.

Some countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, such as India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, show a mix of pink (26-50) and light orange (≤25) for under-five mortality, with varying neonatal mortality rates, including some red circles (18 and 29).

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland and parts of the Sahara desert. "Not applicable" (dark grey) is shown for some small island nations and territories.

[who-whs-2023-p018-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 18]
Child mortality
2 Child mortality statistics are presented here with 90% uncertainty intervals.
Child survival is an important marker of human development – it has been one of the main drivers of increasing global life expectancy over the past 75 years. The international community committed to reducing mortality among the youngest children, setting the SDG target to reduce neonatal mortality (i.e. mortality among newborn babies during the first month of life) by 2030 to at least as low as 12 per 1000 live births, and setting the under-five mortality target (i.e. mortality among children under 5 years of age) for the same period to at least as low as 25 per 1000 live births.
Levels and trends in mortality among children under five years of age

[who-whs-2023-p018-text-001 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 18]
Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

[who-whs-2023-p018-text-003 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 18]
Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. The South-East Asia Region saw a big decline in deaths as the number of neonatal and post-neonatal under-five deaths dropped by 65% and 78%, respectively, between 2000 and 2021.

Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Insufficient finance was a main barrier to implementation of national strategies and plans (Figure 1.17) (48).

Under the Paris Agreement, countries set out their mitigation commitments and adaptation priorities through their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and national adaptation plans (NAPs). The 2023 WHO Review of Health in the NDC report found that over 90% of countries reflect health priorities in their NDCs but only 30% identify the health co-benefits of mitigation action and even fewer (10%) quantify them (47). Health considerations are an integral part of national and international climate policies and processes. As such, health can be a powerful argument to galvanize political and financial support for accelerated climate action.

Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Insufficient finance was a main barrier to implementation of national strategies and plans (Figure 1.17) (48).

[who-whs-2023-p037-text-006 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 37]
Under the Paris Agreement, countries set out their mitigation commitments and adaptation priorities through their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and national adaptation plans (NAPs). The 2023 WHO Review of Health in the NDC report found that over 90% of countries reflect health priorities in their NDCs but only 30% identify the health co-benefits of mitigation action and even fewer (10%) quantify them (47). Health considerations are an integral part of national and international climate policies and processes. As such, health can be a powerful argument to galvanize political and financial support for accelerated climate action.

Panel a. WHO regions (excluding Africa) and global.
The y-axis represents new HIV infections (per 1000 uninfected population), ranging from 0 to 0.5. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.
Legend categories are: Region of the Americas (light blue), Eastern Mediterranean Region (green), European Region (orange), South-East Asia Region (purple), Western Pacific Region (yellow), and Global (dark purple).

Trends:
*   Global (dark purple line) shows a consistent decrease from approximately 0.48 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.
*   South-East Asia Region (purple line) shows a decrease from approximately 0.28 in 2000 to about 0.08 in 2021.
*   Region of the Americas (light blue line) shows a relatively stable trend, starting around 0.22 in 2000 and ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   European Region (orange line) shows an initial decrease, then an increase from around 2007, ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green line) and Western Pacific Region (yellow line) show the lowest rates, both remaining below 0.1 throughout the period, with the Western Pacific Region slightly higher than the Eastern Mediterranean Region.

Panel b. WHO African Region, eastern and southern Africa, western and central Africa and global.
The y-axis represents new HIV infections (per 1000 uninfected population), ranging from 0 to 6.0. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.
Legend categories are: African Region (red), Eastern and southern Africa (light green), Western and central Africa (yellow), and Global (purple).

Trends:
*   Eastern and southern Africa (light green line) shows the highest rates, decreasing significantly from approximately 5.9 in 2000 to about 1.6 in 2021.
*   African Region (red line) shows a decrease from approximately 3.2 in 2000 to about 0.9 in 2021.
*   Western and central Africa (yellow line) shows a decrease from approximately 1.4 in 2000 to about 0.5 in 2021.
*   Global (purple line) shows the lowest rates in this panel, decreasing from approximately 0.5 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.

Overall, all regions and global trends show a decrease in new HIV infections from 2000 to 2021, with African regions having significantly higher rates compared to other WHO regions.

In 2021, there were 1.5 (UI: 1.1–2.0) million new HIV infections globally. This represents a decline of 32% in new HIV infections compared to 2010. The incidence rate (new infections per 1000 uninfected population) declined from 0.32 (UI: 0.24–0.43) in 2010 to 0.19 (UI: 0.15–0.26) in 2021. Across all WHO regions, progress has been strongest in the region with the largest HIV burden, the African Region, with a reduction in the incidence rate of 58% between 2010 and 2021. In western and central Africa, there was a remarkable drop of incidence rates within just one year, from 0.38 (UI: 0.27–0.54) in 2020 to 0.31 (UI: 0.22–0.45) in 2021. In the South-East Asia Region and the Region of the Americas, the incidence rates have decreased since 2010, whereas in the Eastern Mediterranean Region and European Region, the incidence rate has increased since 2010 (Figure 2.1) (2,3).

question: How did the global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 change between 2000 and 2022?

results.text:
Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

* **Left Chart:** Shows "Prevalence (%)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 40). 
* **Right Chart:** Shows "Number (millions)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 250).
* **Legend:** Categories include Stunting (yellow/orange line), Overweight (blue line), Wasting (red point/error bar), and 95% confidence interval (shaded band/error bar).

**Data Values**

*Prevalence (%) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 33.0%; 2022 = 22.3%
* Overweight: 2000 = 5.3%; 2022 = 5.6%
* Wasting: 2022 = 6.8% (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

*Number (millions) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 204.2 million; 2005 = 197.1 million; 2010 = 184.8 million; 2015 = 169.1 million; 2022 = 148.1 million
* Overweight: 2000 = 33.0 million; 2005 = 35.5 million; 2010 = 36.2 million; 2015 = 38.0 million; 2022 = 37.0 million
* Wasting: 2022 = 45.0 million (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

**Main Trends and Comparisons**
* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

*   **Horizontal Axis:** Year from 2000 to 2022 (labelled individually for each year: 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022).

    *   Region of the Americas (light blue line)
    *   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green line)
    *   European Region (orange line)

    *   Western Pacific Region (yellow line)
    *   Global (grey/lavender line)

**Data Values:**
*   No numerical data values are printed as text labels on the data points or lines (values are not labelled).

**Main Trends and Visual Comparisons:**
*   **Direction of Change:** All regions and the global average show a overall downward/declining trend in stunting prevalence from 2000 to 2022.
*   **Highest Prevalence:** South-East Asia Region and African Region have the highest prevalence of stunting across the entire period (around 40–50% in 2000, dropping to around 30% by 2022). South-East Asia begins highest in 2000 and converges with the African Region by 2020–2022.
*   **Lowest Prevalence:** The European Region consistently displays the lowest prevalence of stunting throughout the timeframe (starting slightly above 10% in 2000 and dropping below 10% by 2022), followed closely by the Region of the Americas.
*   **Major Reductions:** The Western Pacific Region and South-East Asia Region show noticeable steep declines over the 2000–2022 period.

These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. Globally, the current tobacco use prevalence

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).
*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

[who-whs-2023-p024-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 24]
Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. Globally, the current tobacco use prevalence

[who-whs-2023-p024-text-002 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 24]
The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

question: In the African Region in 2020, what proportion of the population used safely-managed drinking-water, safely-managed sanitation and a hand-washing facility with soap and water?
answer: In the African Region in 2020, the proportion of the population using safely-managed drinking-water services was 32% [who-whs-2023-p066-fig2.13] [who-whs-2023-p126-table-003], the proportion using safely-managed sanitation services was 23% [who-whs-2023-p066-fig2.13] [who-whs-2023-p126-table-003], and the proportion using a hand-washing facility with soap and water was 28% [who-whs-2023-p066-fig2.13] [who-whs-2023-p127-table-003].

Despite progress, WASH services are still not universally available. Safely managed drinking-water services – i.e. located on premises, available when needed and free from contamination – were accessible by 74% of the global population in 2020, leaving 2 billion people with only basic or limited services or having to rely on unprotected drinking-water sources. Only slightly over half (54%) of the global population were using safely managed sanitation services, with excreta safely disposed on-site or treated off-site. Around 3 in 10 (29%) people worldwide lacked a basic handwashing facility with water and soap at home (37). The coverage of WASH services varies across WHO regions (Figure 2.13), as well as across and within countries.

question: For Mexico, what are life expectancy at birth for both sexes (2019) and the under-five mortality rate (2021)?
answer: For Mexico in 2019, the life expectancy at birth was 73.1 years for males, 78.9 years for females, and 76.0 years for both sexes [who-whs-2023-p100-table-000]. The under-five mortality rate for Mexico in 2021 was 13 per 1000 live births [who-whs-2023-p101-table-000].

results.text: Notably, global life expectancy at birth increased from 46.5 years in 1950 to approximately 73.0 years in 2019 and, despite the setback caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, it is projected to reach 77.0 years by WHO’s 100th anniversary in 2048 (1,2).1 WHO regions such as Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia and Western Pacific – where resources were scarcer and life expectancy was relatively lower in 1950 – have observed the greatest gains, seeing increases in life expectancy of over 30 years between 1950 and 2019. However, progress was slower in WHO’s African Region, which had the second lowest life expectancy at 37.6 years in 1950 but became the region with the lowest life expectancy in 2019 at under 65 years. Nonetheless, the absolute gain in Africa was still greater than that in the Americas where life expectancy increased from 56.0 years in 1950 by about 21 years to 77.2 years in 2019. In contrast, Europe had the highest life expectancy at birth (61.3 years) in 1950 and made the most modest gain of about 17 years by 2019.

Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

question: In the Region of the Americas, what were the prevalence of adult obesity in 2016 and the prevalence of adult hypertension in 2019?

results.text:
Obesity
The age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults aged 18 years or older – i.e. body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m2 – has been rising since the 1970s. In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese, up from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000. The greatest increases occurred in the South-East Asia Region, up from 1.9% (UI: 1.6–2.2%) to 4.7% (UI: 3.9–5.6%) (an almost 150% increase) and the Western Pacific Region, up from 2.7% (UI: 2.4–3.0%) to 6.4% (UI: 5.2–7.7%) (an almost 140% increase). The highest level of adult obesity is 2016 was in the Americas where 28.6% (UI: 26.6–30.5%) of adults were obese, increasing by 42% from 20.2% (UI: 19.0–21.5%) in 2000 (Figure 1.10) (10).

[Vision description] This figure is a multi-panel line chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults (age 18 years or older) across different WHO regions and globally, from 1975 to 2016.

The figure consists of seven panels, each representing a different region or the global average: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

The y-axis for all panels represents "Prevalence (%)" ranging from 0 to 35 in increments of 5. The x-axis for all panels represents years, with labels for 1975, 1985, 1995, 2005, and 2016.

There are three lines in each panel, distinguished by color, representing different categories:
- Light blue line: Both sexes
- Orange line: Male
- Purple line: Female

Main trends and comparisons:
Across all regions and globally, the prevalence of obesity has consistently increased from 1975 to 2016 for both sexes, males, and females.

In most regions, the prevalence of obesity is higher among females than males, with the purple line (Female) generally above the orange line (Male). The light blue line (Both sexes) falls between the male and female lines.

Region-specific observations (approximate values based on visual estimation, as no specific data labels are provided):
- **African Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.
- **Region of the Americas:** Shows the highest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is over 30%, male around 25%, and both sexes around 28%.
- **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 15%, and both sexes around 20%.
- **European Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 20%, and both sexes around 22%.
- **South-East Asia Region:** Shows the lowest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 5%, male around 3%, and both sexes around 4%.
- **Western Pacific Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 7%, male around 5%, and both sexes around 6%.
- **Global:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.

The Region of the Americas consistently shows the highest prevalence of obesity throughout the period, while the South-East Asia Region consistently shows the lowest prevalence. The rate of increase appears steepest in the Region of the Americas and Eastern Mediterranean Region.

Unlike many other health risks, the prevalence rates of obesity were higher among adult women than men. Globally, the femaleto-male ratio of age-standardized prevalence of obesity was 1.4 in 2016, down from 1.6 in 2000 and indicating a more rapid rise in male obesity. The sex difference was greatest in the African Region with a ratio at over 2.7 in 2016, down from 3.7 in 2000. All regions have shown similar trends of the more rapid increase in male obesity and the narrowing gap between sexes, with the regions of Europe and the Western Pacific having a ratio reduced to only 1.1 in 2016.
Obesity and overweight also affects children, and the global prevalence has been increasing since 2000 (11). The latest data on overweight among children under 5 years of age are presented in Section 2.2.

Across all regions and globally, the prevalence of obesity has consistently increased from 1975 to 2016 for both sexes, males, and females.

In most regions, the prevalence of obesity is higher among females than males, with the purple line (Female) generally above the orange line (Male). The light blue line (Both sexes) falls between the male and female lines.

Region-specific observations (approximate values based on visual estimation, as no specific data labels are provided):
- **African Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.
- **Region of the Americas:** Shows the highest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is over 30%, male around 25%, and both sexes around 28%.
- **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 15%, and both sexes around 20%.
- **European Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 20%, and both sexes around 22%.
- **South-East Asia Region:** Shows the lowest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 5%, male around 3%, and both sexes around 4%.
- **Western Pacific Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 7%, male around 5%, and both sexes around 6%.
- **Global:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.

The Region of the Americas consistently shows the highest prevalence of obesity throughout the period, while the South-East Asia Region consistently shows the lowest prevalence. The rate of increase appears steepest in the Region of the Americas and Eastern Mediterranean Region.

[who-whs-2023-p025-text-001 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 25]
Unlike many other health risks, the prevalence rates of obesity were higher among adult women than men. Globally, the femaleto-male ratio of age-standardized prevalence of obesity was 1.4 in 2016, down from 1.6 in 2000 and indicating a more rapid rise in male obesity. The sex difference was greatest in the African Region with a ratio at over 2.7 in 2016, down from 3.7 in 2000. All regions have shown similar trends of the more rapid increase in male obesity and the narrowing gap between sexes, with the regions of Europe and the Western Pacific having a ratio reduced to only 1.1 in 2016.
Obesity and overweight also affects children, and the global prevalence has been increasing since 2000 (11). The latest data on overweight among children under 5 years of age are presented in Section 2.2.

question: What was the average annual rate of reduction of the global under-five mortality rate in 2010-2021, and how many countries will miss the SDG under-five mortality target if that trend continues?
answer: In the 2010–2021 period, the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) of the global under-five mortality rate (U5MR) was 2.7% [who-whs-2023-p019-fig1.4] [who-whs-2023-p018-text-002]. If that trend continues (if the ARR of 2010–2021 remains constant), 54 countries will miss the SDG target for U5MR by 2030 [who-whs-2023-p020-text-000].

[Vision description] This is a line chart titled "Figure 1.4 Trends in the global under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" ranging from 0 to 80.
The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021, with labels at 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2021.
The chart background is divided into two shaded regions: a green-shaded region from 2000 to 2010, and a red-shaded region from 2010 to 2021.

There are two lines in the chart:
- A light blue line represents "U5MR" (under-five mortality rate).
- A purple line represents "NMR" (neonatal mortality rate).

Data values and trends:
For U5MR (light blue line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 4.0%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.7%.
The U5MR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 78 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 38 per 1000 live births in 2021.

For NMR (purple line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 3.2%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.2%.
The NMR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 30 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 18 per 1000 live births in 2021.

Overall trends:
Both U5MR and NMR show a decreasing trend from 2000 to 2021.
The rate of reduction for both U5MR and NMR was higher in the 2000-2010 period compared to the 2010-2021 period.
U5MR is consistently higher than NMR throughout the entire period.

Globally, NMR declined at a slower rate compared to U5MR, and both declined more slowly during the second decade (2010–2021) compared to the first decade (2000–2009). The ARR of the NMR dropped from 3.2% during 2000–2009 to 2.2% during 2010–2021, while the ARR of U5MR fell from 4.0% during the first period to 2.7% during the second period (Figure 1.4). This slowdown has been particularly pronounced since the start of the SDG era in 2015.

Interventions to prevent child deaths
If current trends continue – i.e. if the ARR of 2010–2021 remains constant – 54 countries will not meet the SDG target for U5MR and 63 countries will not meet the target for NMR by 2030. Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

However, the rapid progress commonly observed for many of these indicators in the era of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) has markedly stalled since 2015, challenging the timely attainment of the SDG targets by 2030. This is evidenced by the falling annual rate of reduction in indicators such as the maternal mortality ratio, under-five and neonatal mortality rates, premature mortality from major NCDs, and suicide and road traffic mortality rates. Almost halfway through the SDG era, some of these indicators are far from reaching the midpoint of the required trajectories to reach their respective SDG targets.

question: What share of adults globally were obese in 2016, and how did that compare with 2000?
answer: In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese [who-whs-2023-p025-text-000]. This was an increase from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000 [who-whs-2023-p025-text-000].

events.query: share of adults globally obese 2016 2000

results.text:
Obesity
The age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults aged 18 years or older – i.e. body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m2 – has been rising since the 1970s. In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese, up from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000. The greatest increases occurred in the South-East Asia Region, up from 1.9% (UI: 1.6–2.2%) to 4.7% (UI: 3.9–5.6%) (an almost 150% increase) and the Western Pacific Region, up from 2.7% (UI: 2.4–3.0%) to 6.4% (UI: 5.2–7.7%) (an almost 140% increase). results.text:
Nevertheless, reported deaths due to COVID-19 generally underestimate the true toll of the impact of COVID-19 on human mortality. Over the past two years, WHO has undertaken a monumental effort to collate all available information on reported all-cause mortality by week and month both during and before the pandemic. The Organization also collated data and other relevant information on the COVID-19 pandemic itself as well as the relevant epidemiological situation of populations around the world to produce for its Member States the most comprehensive assessment of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on mortality by sex and age for 2020 and 2021 (23,24).
Through the Member State consultation conducted in 2023, WHO’s updated estimates of excess mortality show that globally 14.9 million (95% UI: 13.3–16.6 million) excess deaths could be attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic by the end of 2021. More excess deaths occurred in 2021 – 10.4 million (95%

The large discrepancy between estimated global excess mortality and the reported deaths due to COVID-19 – a difference of 9.4 million by the end of 2021 – shows that the impact of the pandemic is far-reaching. Indeed, 162 out of 194 WHO Member States show a higher excess mortality rate associated with the COVID-19 pandemic than the reported mortality rate attributable to COVID-19 between 2020 and 2021.

Age and sex distributions in the excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic
While a total of 14.9 million estimated excess deaths was associated with the COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2021, the age distribution of the COVID-19-related excess mortality shows that the pandemic disproportionally affected the age group of 45 years and above (14.2 million or 95% of the global excess deaths). While 0.7 million excess deaths were observed in the age group of 25–44 years (5% of the global excess deaths), fewer deaths than expected (about 37 000 fewer deaths) were estimated to have occurred among people under the age of 25 years. An estimated 31% of the global excess deaths occurred in ages between 45 and 64 years (i.e. 4.6 million). Similarly, 46% of global excess deaths (i.e. 6.8 million) occurred between 65 and 84 years. The oldest age group, 85 years and above, accounted for 18% of excess deaths globally (i.e. 2.7 million) (25).

UI: 9.1–12.1 million) – than in 2020 when there was a total of 4.4 million (UI: 3.9–5.0 million). At the regional level, the South- East Asia Region had the highest number of excess deaths for the years 2020 and 2021 at 6.1 million (UI: 4.7–7.8 million), which account for 41% of global excess deaths; this was significantly different from the percentage of globally reported COVID-19 deaths that the South-East Asia Region accounted for over the same period (13.3% of global reported deaths). Except for the Western Pacific Region and the African Region, which had only 0.2 million (UI: 0.0–0.4 million) and 0.8 million (UI: 0.5–1.1 million) estimated excess deaths respectively, all other regions had estimated excess deaths of more than 1 million by the end of 2021. The large discrepancy between estimated global excess mortality and the reported deaths due to COVID-19 – a difference of 9.4 million by the end of 2021 – shows that the impact of the pandemic is far-reaching. question: Since 2016, for how many countries has the availability and affordability of a core set of essential medicines been estimated, and what was the median value?
answer: Since 2016, the availability and affordability of a core set of relevant essential medicines has been estimated for 17 countries, with a median value across all 17 countries of 15% (IQR: 0–28%) [who-whs-2023-p077-text-000].

events.query: availability and affordability of a core set of essential medicines 2016 median

results.text: Access to essential medicines – a multidimensional concept which combines both the affordability and availability of medicines – is another key component for achieving UHC. Since 2016, the proportion of health facilities that have a core set of relevant essential medicines available and affordable on a sustainable basis has been estimated for 17 countries across WHO’s African, Americas and European regions, with a median value across all 17 countries of 15% (IQR: 0–28%) (77). The sparsity of data and lack of mechanisms for tracking progress make the interpretation of this particular metric difficult. During the COVID-19 pandemic, people suffering from NCDs, such as cancer, heart diseases and diabetes, reported disruptions or sustained challenges in accessing their routine medications for these diseases (78).

Since 2016, the proportion of health facilities that have a core set of relevant essential medicines available and affordable on a sustainable basis has been estimated for 17 countries across WHO’s African, Americas and European regions, with a median value across all 17 countries of 15% (IQR: 0–28%) (77). The sparsity of data and lack of mechanisms for tracking progress make the interpretation of this particular metric difficult. During the COVID-19 pandemic, people suffering from NCDs, such as cancer, heart diseases and diabetes, reported disruptions or sustained challenges in accessing their routine medications for these diseases (78).

question: What was the global male-to-female ratio of tobacco use prevalence in 2020, and how had it changed since 2000?
answer: The global male-to-female ratio of current tobacco use prevalence was 4.7 in 2020 [who-whs-2023-p024-text-002]. This had risen from 3.0 in 2000, indicating a slower reduction in tobacco use among men compared to women [who-whs-2023-p024-text-002].

events.query: global male-to-female ratio of tobacco use prevalence 2020 2000

results.text: The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Poliomyelitis is a highly infectious viral disease that primarily affects children under 5 years of age. WPV cases have decreased by over 99% since the launch of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988 – from an estimated 350 000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to six reported cases in 2021 (24).
Of the three strains of WPV (types 1, 2 and 3), type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 was declared eradicated in 2019. Only type 1 WPV remains. In 2022, 20 WPV type 1 cases were reported in Pakistan, two cases in Afghanistan and eight cases in Mozambique (25).
Interrupting transmission of WPV1 and circulating vaccinederived poliovirus type 2 is the primary goal on the path to global polio eradication (26).

[Vision description] **Figure Type and Layout**
Figure 2.14 is a combination Pareto-style chart featuring blue vertical bar charts (representing Mortality rate) overlaid with a purple line graph (representing Cumulative share of number of deaths) across WHO regions for the year 2019. 

* **Horizontal Axis (WHO regions):** African Region, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, European Region.
* **Left Vertical Axis (Mortality rate):** Measured in "per 100 000 population", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 50 in increments of 10.
* **Right Vertical Axis (Cumulative share):** Measured in "Cumulative share of number of deaths (%)", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 100% in increments of 20%.
* **Legend:** 
  * Blue bar: Mortality rate
  * Purple line: Cumulative share of number of deaths

**Data Values**
* Individual numerical values for each region's mortality rate and cumulative percentage share are not printed directly as text labels on the chart elements.

**Main Visible Trends and Comparisons**
* **Mortality Rate:** The African Region has the highest mortality rate per 100,000 population, followed by the South-East Asia Region and the Eastern Mediterranean Region. The Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, and European Region have substantially lower mortality rates.
* **Cumulative Share of Deaths:** The purple line demonstrates that the top two regions (African Region and South-East Asia Region) account for approximately 80% of the cumulative share of total deaths attributed to exposure to unsafe WASH services.

Poliomyelitis caused by WPV
Poliomyelitis is a highly infectious viral disease that primarily affects children under 5 years of age. WPV cases have decreased by over 99% since the launch of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988 – from an estimated 350 000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to six reported cases in 2021 (24).
Of the three strains of WPV (types 1, 2 and 3), type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 was declared eradicated in 2019. Only type 1 WPV remains. In 2022, 20 WPV type 1 cases were reported in Pakistan, two cases in Afghanistan and eight cases in Mozambique (25).
Interrupting transmission of WPV1 and circulating vaccinederived poliovirus type 2 is the primary goal on the path to global polio eradication (26).

results.text: Notably, global life expectancy at birth increased from 46.5 years in 1950 to approximately 73.0 years in 2019 and, despite the setback caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, it is projected to reach 77.0 years by WHO’s 100th anniversary in 2048 (1,2).1 WHO regions such as Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia and Western Pacific – where resources were scarcer and life expectancy was relatively lower in 1950 – have observed the greatest gains, seeing increases in life expectancy of over 30 years between 1950 and 2019. However, progress was slower in WHO’s African Region, which had the second lowest life expectancy at 37.6 years in 1950 but became the region with the lowest life expectancy in 2019 at under 65 years. Nonetheless, the absolute gain in Africa was still greater than that in the Americas where life expectancy increased from 56.0 years in 1950 by about 21 years to 77.2 years in 2019. In contrast, Europe had the highest life expectancy at birth (61.3 years) in 1950 and made the most modest gain of about 17 years by 2019.

  - HPV (green line)
  - MCV2 (red line)

- **PCV3:** Data begins in 2008 at under 10% and increases consistently to around 50% by 2020 and 2021.
- **HPV:** Represents the lowest immunization rate of the group; data begins in 2010 at near 0% and increases gradually to peak slightly above 10% in 2019 before stabilizing around 10% in 2020 and 2021.

answer: Không đủ bằng chứng để trả lời.

events.query: drowning worldwide deaths 2019

results.text:
•2.3 Injuries and violence
Global death rates due to injuries declined by 20% during the period 2000–2019 – from 71.7 (UI: 53.8–93.8) deaths per 100 000 population to 57.4 (UI: 38.7–81.4) deaths per 100 000 population. Over this period, injuries caused about 8% of all deaths. In 2019, deaths due to road traffic injuries made up 29% of all injury deaths, followed by suicide and falls (each causing 16% of all injury deaths), and homicide (11% of all injury deaths) (29).
The suicide rate fell by 29% globally between 2000 and 2019, from 13.0 (UI: 10.4–16.0) to 9.2 (UI: 9.7–12.6) deaths per 100 000 population (Figure 2.11). In all WHO regions, suicide rates have been on the decline, except in the Region of the Americas where the rate rose by 28%. The greatest decline (42%) was seen in the European Region, although the suicide rate in 2019 remained the highest at 12.8 (UI 10.1–16.4) deaths per 100 000 population.

Globally in 2019, an estimated 1.4 million deaths – equivalent to 2.5% of all deaths that year – could have been prevented with safe WASH. These include deaths due to diarrhoea, acute respiratory infections, soil-transmitted helminthiases and undernutrition. Almost all (97%) of these deaths were in low- and middle-income countries, with 79% in the African and South- East Asia regions (Figure 2.14). The African Region suffered the highest mortality rate at 46.7 deaths per 100 000 population – over 10 times the rates in the Western Pacific and European regions. At 29.6 deaths per 100 000, the mortality rate in the South-East Asia Region was 62% higher than the global average of 18.3 deaths per 100 000 population (43).

Globally, men are about twice as likely to die from injury than women are. The death rates due to all injuries in 2019 were 77.6 (UI: 52.7–109.1) deaths per 100 000 male population and 36.9 (UI: 24.4–53.2) deaths per 100 000 female population. Across WHO regions and among the three injury causes discussed in this section, the male-to-female ratio of death rates in 2019 was highest for homicide in the Region of the Americas, where the death rate among men and boys was over seven times that among women and girls.

The global death rate due to homicides declined by 22% over the same period. However, progress varied greatly across WHO regions, with the homicide rate in the European Region declining by 63% while that in the Region of the Americas stayed roughly the same. In 2019, the homicide rate of 19.2 (UI: 15.6–23.7) deaths per 100 000 population in the Region of the Americas was over three times the global average of 6.2 (UI: 4.0–8.7) deaths per 100 000 population).

Figure 2.14 Mortality rate and cumulative share of deaths attributed to exposure to unsafe WASH services, by WHO region, 2019
[Text layer in figure] Figure 2.14 Mortality rate and cumulative share of deaths attributed to exposure to unsafe WASH services, by WHO region, 2019 0 10 20 30 40 50 Mortality rate (per 100 000 population) 0 20 40 60 80 100 Cumulative share of number of deaths (%) Mortality rate Cumulative share of number of deaths African Region South-East Asia Region Eastern Mediterranean Region Region of the Americas Western Paciﬁc Region European Region Source: Ref. (43).
[Vision description] **Figure Type and Layout**
Figure 2.14 is a combination Pareto-style chart featuring blue vertical bar charts (representing Mortality rate) overlaid with a purple line graph (representing Cumulative share of number of deaths) across WHO regions for the year 2019. 

* **Horizontal Axis (WHO regions):** African Region, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, European Region.
* **Left Vertical Axis (Mortality rate):** Measured in "per 100 000 population", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 50 in increments of 10.
* **Right Vertical Axis (Cumulative share):** Measured in "Cumulative share of number of deaths (%)", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 100% in increments of 20%.
* **Legend:** 
  * Blue bar: Mortality rate
  * Purple line: Cumulative share of number of deaths

**Data Values**
* Individual numerical values for each region's mortality rate and cumulative percentage share are not printed directly as text labels on the chart elements.

**Main Visible Trends and Comparisons**
* **Mortality Rate:** The African Region has the highest mortality rate per 100,000 population, followed by the South-East Asia Region and the Eastern Mediterranean Region. The Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, and European Region have substantially lower mortality rates.
* **Cumulative Share of Deaths:** The purple line demonstrates that the top two regions (African Region and South-East Asia Region) account for approximately 80% of the cumulative share of total deaths attributed to exposure to unsafe WASH services.

results.text:
In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy on viral hepatitis which calls for the elimination of viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030 (18). In 2022, the Seventy-fifth World Health Assembly noted a new set of integrated global health sector strategies on HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections for the period 2022–2030 that would aim to achieve this goal. Progress is measured by a set of global targets and milestones for 2025 and 2030. Figure 2.6 shows the projected impact of the strategies in reducing the incidence and mortality of hepatitis B (19).
Globally in 2019, 296 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B (defined as hepatitis B surface antigen positive) – which included 1.5 million new infections – and resulted in approximately 820 000 deaths, mainly from cirrhosis and primary liver cancer (20).

20. Global progress report on HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, 2021. Accountability for the global health sector strategies 2016–2021: actions for impact. Geneva: World Health Organization; June 2021 (https://apps.who.int/iris/ handle/10665/341412, accessed 7 March 2023.
21. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence among children under 5 years. Global Health Observatory data. Geneva: World Health Organization (https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/indicators/indicator-details/GHO/hepatitis-b-surface-antigen- (hbsag)-prevalence-among-children-under-5-years, accessed 7 March 2023).
22. Ending the neglect to attain the sustainable development goals: a road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021–2030. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2020 (https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/338565, accessed 8 March 2023).

h World malaria report 2022. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022 (https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/365169,
accessed 30 April 2023). “-” indicates countries or regions that are malaria-free.
i Global and country estimates of immunization coverage and chronic HBV infection. Geneva: World Health Organization (http:// situatedlaboratories.net/who-hepB-dashboard/src/#global-strategies, accessed 30 April 2023).
j Neglected tropical diseases [online database]. Global Health Observatory (GHO) data. Geneva: World Health Organization (https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/topic-details/GHO/neglected-tropical-diseases, accessed 30 April 2023). Global and regional aggregates include imputation of incomplete reports.
k Global health estimates 2019: deaths by cause, age, sex, by country and by region, 2000–2019. Geneva: World Health

In addition to the goal of reducing the number of annual new hepatitis B infections to 170 000 new cases and mortality to 310 000 deaths by 2030, another important target is to reduce the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to below 0.1% in children aged 5 years.
The latest available data show that the HBsAg prevalence among children under 5 years was 0.94% (UI: 0.82–1.06) globally in 2020. Prevalence is lowest in the Region of the Americas at 0.07% (UI: 0.05–0.13) and highest in the WHO African Region at 2.53% (UI: 2.10–3.07) (21).
Efforts to achieve the 2030 target include early diagnosis and treatment of persons living with hepatitis B, a timely birth dose of hepatitis vaccine to prevent vertical transmission from mother to child, and hepatitis B vaccine coverage among children (third dose).

In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy on viral hepatitis which calls for the elimination of viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030 (18). In 2022, the Seventy-fifth World Health Assembly noted a new set of integrated global health sector strategies on HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections for the period 2022–2030 that would aim to achieve this goal. Progress is measured by a set of global targets and milestones for 2025 and 2030. Figure 2.6 shows the projected impact of the strategies in reducing the incidence and mortality of hepatitis B (19).
Globally in 2019, 296 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B (defined as hepatitis B surface antigen positive) – which included 1.5 million new infections – and resulted in approximately 820 000 deaths, mainly from cirrhosis and primary liver cancer (20).

In addition to the goal of reducing the number of annual new hepatitis B infections to 170 000 new cases and mortality to 310 000 deaths by 2030, another important target is to reduce the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to below 0.1% in children aged 5 years.
The latest available data show that the HBsAg prevalence among children under 5 years was 0.94% (UI: 0.82–1.06) globally in 2020. Prevalence is lowest in the Region of the Americas at 0.07% (UI: 0.05–0.13) and highest in the WHO African Region at 2.53% (UI: 2.10–3.07) (21).
Efforts to achieve the 2030 target include early diagnosis and treatment of persons living with hepatitis B, a timely birth dose of hepatitis vaccine to prevent vertical transmission from mother to child, and hepatitis B vaccine coverage among children (third dose).
